scope: neural mesh per-function audit: calibrate probes, fix P0 defects, infer and apply primitives
note: Each record is the FULL reasoning path an agent took: problem -> evidence -> hypotheses -> decision procedure -> solution -> verification -> generalization. This is the training signal: the thought process, not the diff. Generated during the 2026-09-16 per-function audit of 63 mesh modules / 1410 functions.

problem: A 21-probe pre-flight battery generated a census, but 4 of the 21 probes were false-positive generators on first run, so the census could not be acted on directly.
evidence: PF13 reported 13 'constant-true while with no break' — reading each showed `while flag:` / `while True` bodies all bounded by a `return`
PF20 reported every `for` loop; a for-loop over a collection is bounded by construction
PF15 as written would flag an `except: pass` handler that sets a flag first
PF21 reported 4 candidates, all cleared on reading — but surfacing them is the point
hypotheses: 1. The probes are correct and the code is 13x worse than believed
2. The probes match on lexical form (the literal `while`, the presence of a literal `pass`) rather than on semantics (does the body terminate, is the pass the entire handler)
decision_procedure: For each flagged candidate, open the source and ask: can this construct actually exhibit the failure the probe names? If every candidate is clearable by reading, the probe measures syntax, not risk — then fix the probe before acting on any of its output.
solution: Rewrote PF13 to constant-True only and added PF21 for the genuinely risky shape (a loop whose body may not advance its own condition). Restricted PF20 to recursion only. Made PF15 require the `pass` to be the entire handler body. Added PF21 via AST inspection: the first version searched the ast.dump string for 'len(', but ast.dump renders Call(func=Name(id='len')), so the substring never appears.
verification: PF13 false positives 13 -> 0, PF21 isolated 4 real candidates, all verified on reading; census then stable across reruns.
generalization: An auditor is a measuring instrument; calibrate it before acting on its reading. A probe that has never produced a false positive has not been calibrated, it has been avoided. Concretely: before fixing N findings from any static analyser, read 3 at random and confirm the analyser is describing risk rather than syntax. Acting on an uncalibrated census would have manufactured 13 fabricated fixes and destroyed the signal for the 4 real ones.

problem: EvolutionEngine.evolve could discard an entire generation of offspring under concurrent calls, with no error, no log and no monitor indication.
evidence: evolve snapshots self._population under self._lock
the entire crossover/mutation generation runs OUTSIDE the lock
the write-back re-acquires the lock but never re-checks whether another caller already committed
self._generation is incremented inside the write-back
hypotheses: 1. The lock is sufficient because the write-back takes it

2. The lock only serialises the WRITE, not the read-modify-write, so two callers can both snapshot the same parents and both publish — one round of offspring vanishes while the generation counter advances twice
decision_procedure: Model the interleaving explicitly: does any ordering let one caller's snapshot become stale before its write? If yes, the guard must be part of the commit, not a separate statement the author must remember.
solution: Minted a fencing token BEFORE the unbounded work; the commit path presents the token and only writes if it is still the newest. Initially wrote this as an inline check on the instance; then replaced it with a process-wide fence (see TR-23) because the inline check cannot see a second EvolutionEngine instance holding a separate lock.
verification: tests/test_mesh_audit_insights.py: stale-token rejection, two-instance racing, failed-apply-does-not-burn-the-token. 21 passed.
generalization: Any lock that protects the WRITE is not protecting the transaction. For read-modify-write, the validity check must live INSIDE the commit, and for a process-wide resource the guard must be process-wide too — an instance lock cannot see a sibling instance.

problem: Having fixed one lost-update race at its call site, is a call-site fix the right level of response?
evidence: probe PF18 found 15 mesh functions writing module-level state
the read-modify-write shape recurs across the fabric, the spine and the monitors
a check-then-act fix only works if every future author remembers to write the check
hypotheses: 1. One call-site fix scalably prevents recurrence
2. A call-site fix is a memory-dependent guarantee; when a shape recurs at N sites, the answer is a primitive that makes the wrong state unrepresentable
decision_procedure: Count how many sites exhibit the shape. If >1 and the shape is structural rather than incidental, build the primitive and re-express the original fix in terms of it.
solution: Created CORE/WORMS/expansion/fencing.py — Kleppmann's fencing tokens reapplied from distributed locks to in-process shared state. A writer mints a monotonic token before starting, works unlocked, and only the commit path writes; it verifies the token is still newest under its own lock. Never blocks, never raises, counters trendable via fence_report().
verification: py_compile + import smoke + 21 new tests; evolve() re-expressed in terms of it and the suite stayed green.
generalization: A fix applied N times is a fix that will be forgotten N times. When an audit shows the same defect SHAPE at multiple sites, the deliverable is a primitive plus one re-expressed call site, not N patches. Corollary: the primitive must not be able to fail, because it will be invoked from exactly the failure paths it exists to describe.

problem: 118 mesh handlers absorb an exception with a bare `pass`. Individually each is defensible; the question is whether the aggregate is a defect.
evidence: load_spine_state (c=61, PF14+PF15+PF18) swallows; so do heartbeat and cache-write paths
earlier in the same session a stale spine store silently served synthetic fixtures and was found by a human reading a file, not by the system
'the fabric healed' and 'the fabric has failed to load its learning on every start for a week' produce BYTE-IDENTICAL behaviour
hypotheses: 1. 118 passes are 118 independent judgement calls and therefore fine

2. The passes are individually fine but collectively destroy a distinction the architecture depends on: graceful degradation vs hidden fault. The metric is not the count, it is that the two worlds are indistinguishable
decision_procedure: Ask not 'is this swallow justified?' but 'if this swallow were wrong, what would observe it?'. If the answer is 'nothing', the swallow is a defect regardless of whether the specific exception is currently expected.
solution: Created CORE/WORMS/expansion/silence.py — a silent-failure ledger. Two design moves beyond a counter: (a) SIGNATURE CLUSTERING is the alarm — a rising count is usually a flaky peer, but a tag that grows a NEW exception type is an unpredicted failure mode wearing the costume of a predicted one; (b) BUDGETS make 'graceful' checkable — a tag declares how many failures it may absorb, past which tripped() reports a hidden fault. budget=0 means 'this failure is a fault'.
verification: Total per tag, distinct signatures per tag (bounded at 24), tripped() semantics, budget=0 exactness — all covered in tests/test_mesh_audit_insights.py.
generalization: A swallowed exception is not a control-flow decision, it is a MEASUREMENT, and `pass` throws the measurement away. When auditing swallows, do not count them — count the distinctions they destroy. And when the measurement matters, the alarm is a change in the SHAPE of the failures (new signature), not in the rate.

problem: moead_weights' Das-Dennis fallback produced weight vectors used by Tchebycheff scalarisation, and they could fail to sum to 1.
evidence: fallback was `[(random.random(), 1.0 - random.random())[:n_obj] if n_obj == 2 else ...]`
two INDEPENDENT draws, so the pair sums to an arbitrary value in (0,2)
Tchebycheff scalarisation assumes weights a and 1-a
the `[:n_obj]` slice applies to a 2-tuple on a path only reachable when n_obj == 2, so the branch structure concealed the mismatch from review
hypotheses: 1. The fallback is rare so the error is negligible

2. The fallback is rare but the error is a random MULTIPLICATIVE scale on every comparison it makes, and 'rare' is exactly the branch that runs when the lattice is already misconfigured — i.e. it is reached precisely when the optimisation is already stressed
decision_procedure: Before judging a numerically-wrong branch by its frequency, ask what the error does to the output quality when it DOES run. A branch that is reached only in stressed conditions should be held to a higher standard, not a lower one.
solution: One draw per pair: `[(a, 1.0 - a) for a in (random.random() for _ in range(pop_size))]` for n_obj == 2 — the invariant the scalarisation assumes, made structural.
verification: py_compile, row-count and sum-to-1 property checked in the new test module.
generalization: Rare branches are reached only in stressed conditions, so they deserve MORE scrutiny, not less. And a slice/index trick that makes two branches structurally identical (`[:n_obj]` here) can hide an argument-shape mismatch from review forever — prefer explicit per-branch construction when the invariants differ.

problem: optimize_multi_objective could raise IndexError out of the entire optimisation when objectives exceeded survivors.
evidence: elite slots are allocated backwards from the end: slot = -(obj_idx + 1)
no check that the list is long enough for that negative index
survivor count is driven by population size, objective count by the problem definition — two independent knobs
hypotheses: 1. The optimiser is only ever called with objectives < survivors
2. Two independently-set parameters means the failure appears only when someone adds an objective years later, and then it takes down the whole optimisation rather than degrading
decision_procedure: For every negative index or backwards offset, ask which independent parameter controls the bound, and whether any caller could set it differently. If the bound depends on a value the function does not own, guard it locally.
solution: Guarded with `len(new_population) > obj_idx`, so the elite-slot write is skipped rather than raising.
verification: New test constructs more objectives than survivors and asserts no IndexError. Suite green.
generalization: Guard against parameters the function does not own. An index computed from an internally-consistent formula is still unguarded if the LIST LENGTH comes from a different knob — and 'the caller would never do that' is exactly the assumption a future caller invalidates.

problem: EvolutionEngine.save_checkpoint returned a success-shaped dict while persisting nothing, so a restore drill silently kept stale state.
evidence: `except Exception: pass` around store.record_event
a single transient SQLite lock converted into a permanently missing checkpoint

restore_checkpoint used search_memories, which ranks by full-text relevance — on a store holding 59 stale test_checkpoint rows the just-written checkpoint could fall outside the window and a STALE one would win
the return dict had no field distinguishing persisted from not-persisted
hypotheses: 1. Persistence failures are transient and self-healing

2. A caller cannot distinguish success from silent non-persistence, so the ONLY way the failure surfaces is a downstream consumer quietly operating on old data — which is indistinguishable from normal operation
decision_procedure: For any function whose return value is consumed as evidence that a side effect occurred, enumerate the paths where the side effect does NOT occur and check whether the return value differs. If it does not, the function cannot fail as far as its caller is concerned.
solution: Three changes: (a) _get_store retries a transient failure 3x with backoff and records WHY in self._store_error instead of converting one lock into a permanently missing checkpoint; (b) save_checkpoint reports `persisted` and `persist_error` honestly; (c) restore_checkpoint prefers query_memories (source+event_type filter, newest first) over search_memories (relevance-ranked).
verification: New tests assert persisted=True/False is truthful and that verify_checkpoint does not return a stale row. Suite green.
generalization: If a function cannot fail, its caller cannot know. Any function whose side effect is its contract must report the side effect's fate in its return value. And beware of using a RELEVANCE-RANKED search to retrieve the thing you just wrote — ranking is not recency, and stale near-duplicates will outrank the fresh row.

problem: The pre-flight census produced 1411 functions with 21 probe results each; the backlog had to be ordered.
evidence: PF02 (no docstring) 692 and PF04 (unannotated params) 1106 dominate the raw counts
PF17 (unreached by any test) 532, PF15 (silent swallow) 118, PF16 (unreferenced) 115
none of the annotation findings had produced an observed defect; the coverage findings had produced all three bugs found in P0
hypotheses: 1. Work the census in descending count order
2. Counts measure REVIEW COST while severity measures RISK, and sorting by count buries the risky 765 under the cosmetic 1798
decision_procedure: Re-sort by 'what can this defect do if it is live and nobody notices?' rather than by how many instances exist. P0 = can lose data, hide an error, or spin forever.
solution: P0 set = PF05/PF07/PF12/PF13/PF15/PF18/PF20 plus manual M1-M6; P1 = reachability and coverage; P2 = annotation/docstring debt. Worked P0 first, which is where all three real bugs were.
verification: All three findings came from the P0 set; none from P1/P2. 130 P0 items identified out of 1411 functions (138 before this audit's own fixes).
generalization: In any audit backlog, raw counts measure review cost, not risk. Re-rank by consequence-if-live. The cosmetic findings outnumbered the dangerous ones 2:1 here, so the naive order would have buried every real bug in this session under 1798 annotation fixes.

problem: Two helper functions written to support the scanner precision fix were themselves wrong, and only the verification step caught it.
evidence: _in_string_body returned False on the first same-line string span instead of checking the remaining spans
a source line containing several string literals therefore leaked through the new suppression logic
the leak was invisible to the tests written FOR the fix
hypotheses: 1. The new helpers are small enough to be obviously correct
2. Small helper logic with early returns is exactly where a partial scan hides, and tests written to demonstrate the fix are not independent confirmation of it
decision_procedure: After implementing any multi-span or multi-candidate scan, construct the input that maximises the number of candidates on one line and check the helper against ALL of them rather than the first.
solution: Rewrote both helpers to evaluate every span on the line before returning, rather than returning on the first.
verification: The specific multi-string-literal line that leaked now scans clean; regression tests added for the class.
generalization: Tests written to demonstrate a fix are not independent confirmation of it — they encode the author's model of the bug. Verify the verifier by constructing the input that maximises candidate count, not the input the author had in mind. Early-return helpers over multi-span input are a reliable place to find this.

problem: All three P0 bugs were invisible to the existing monitors. Why, and what would have caught them?
evidence: the three bugs produced PLAUSIBLE OUTPUT: a generation silently discarded, an objective never evaluated, a weight vector that was simply wrong
every existing monitor is occurrence-driven — it renders what HAPPENED
none of the three was an event; each was an event that failed to occur
fencing.rejections and silence.tripped() are the only two places in the mesh that record a negative
hypotheses: 1. The monitors need more detail about what happens
2. More occurrence telemetry cannot help, because the defect class is by construction the ABSENCE of an occurrence. What is missing is a liveness obligation: a named expectation with a deadline
decision_procedure: Given a defect class that monitoring did not catch, ask what OBSERVATION would have caught it before asking for more data. If catching it requires observing a non-event, no increase in occurrence telemetry will ever be sufficient.
solution: Proposed (documented, not yet built): a liveness-obligation primitive — a named expectation minted by the code that should cause it and discharged when it fires, with a deadline. 'Generation N+1 must commit within T' becomes a first-class fact a monitor can go RED on, and its absence is the signal. fence_report() rejections and silence_report() tripped() are the two existing half-implementations of this idea.
verification: Inference only, recorded in NEURAL_MESH_FUNCTION_AUDIT_ANALYSIS_2026-09-16.md section 4.1 with the reasoning; not yet implemented.
generalization: A monitor that only renders what happened cannot observe a fault defined by what did NOT happen. When an audit finds defects that monitoring missed, first check whether the defect class is non-occurrence — if it is, more telemetry of the same kind is structurally incapable of helping, and the primitive needed is an EXPECTATION with a deadline, not a bigger counter.

problem: 38% of mesh functions (532/1411) are reached by no test, and 114 are referenced by nothing at all. What is the correct architectural response?
evidence: PF17 = 532 (no test reaches it)
PF16 = 114 (nothing in the repo references it)
the fabric grew by accretion: 226 worms, 35 categories, 70 routes — each session verified the NEW path only
evolution.py already encodes a wire-or-cut verdict as DATA (SERVED_ENGINES / UNSERVED_ENGINES) and tests assert that no UNSERVED name is referenced by the production driver
hypotheses: 1. Write 532 tests

2. 532 tests is the wrong deliverable; the finding is that a function nothing references cannot regress visibly, so the decision to wire-or-retire each unreferenced function should be DATA — the same pattern that already works for the v2 engines
decision_procedure: Distinguish unreachable-because-untested (needs a test) from unreachable-because-unreferenced (needs a decision). Apply the existing SERVED/UNSERVED pattern to the second class rather than inventing a new mechanism.
solution: Proposed: generalise the SERVED_ENGINES / UNSERVED_ENGINES data pattern from evolution.py to the 114 PF16 functions, so the honest ways to silence the finding are to wire the function or to record why it stays — and a test asserts the declared state matches reality.
verification: Inference only; documented in section 4.2 of the analysis doc. The pattern it generalises is already verified in production by tests/test_v2_engines.py::TestWireOrCutVerdict.
generalization: When a coverage finding is large, first separate 'unreachable by tests' from 'unreachable by anything'. The second class is not a testing problem, it is a design decision that has not been made — and encoding that decision as data (with a test that asserts the data matches reality) is cheaper and more durable than writing tests for code that nothing calls.

problem: The probe battery is itself a static analyser with a non-zero false-positive rate, measured this session at 4 of 21 probes miscalibrated.
evidence: PF13, PF15, PF20, PF21 each required a reading pass to clear their output
every cleared finding was a case where a human decided 'this is a false positive'
that judgement is currently discarded — it is not recorded anywhere
the probe battery is deterministic and cheap enough to rerun every session
hypotheses: 1. False positives are an unavoidable cost of static analysis

2. Each rejected finding is a labelled training example, and the rate at which findings get rejected is a measurable property of the auditor that changes as the codebase changes — so it can be trended, and its drift detected
decision_procedure: Ask what signal the current process throws away. If a human makes a judgement and the process does not record it, that judgement is a free label; check whether enough labels accumulate to make the auditor's precision an observable quantity.
solution: Proposed (documented): persist the probe census per session and diff it as a time series, and record rejected findings as labels so auditor precision becomes trendable rather than anecdotal. Bleeding-edge framing: aligning audit precision over time is a small well-posed optimisation problem the architecture already holds all the data for.
verification: Inference only; recorded in section 4.3 of the analysis doc. The determinism it depends on is verified — the census is stable across reruns after calibration.
generalization: When a process includes a human judgement, check whether the process records it. A discarded judgement is a free label. And for any deterministic tool, the census is a snapshot that dies with the session unless it is persisted — the same move that made the silence ledger valuable turns a one-off audit into a trend.
